claims.text: Coupled tribo-corrosion degradation in high-entropy alloys is governed by a dynamic equilibrium between mechanical passive-film removal and film regeneration.
The passive film is a compositionally complex, protective multi-element oxide.
Inherent sluggish diffusion in the HEA promotes rapid, self-healing regeneration of the passive oxide.
Synergistic elemental interactions promote continuous formation of a stable multi-element oxide layer.
Continuous oxide reformation limits localized corrosion even when wear partially abrades the film.
An otherwise comparable composition lacking regenerative oxide capability will undergo accelerated coupled degradation.
The initially prepared HEA surface carries a thin, naturally formed passive oxide layer.
A stable Cr-, Al-, or Mn-rich passive oxide can repair wear-induced surface damage.
Mechanical wear periodically removes the passive film and exposes fresh alloy substrate.
High-entropy effects and stable elemental oxides cause rapid re-oxidation of exposed substrate.
When oxide reformation is sufficiently rapid, corrosion remains limited despite mechanical damage.
When oxide reformation is too slow, aggressive corrosion of exposed substrate weakens surface integrity and exacerbates wear.
Relative to a matched non-regenerative baseline, the HEA will have a lower total mass-loss rate and shallower wear track during tribo-corrosion.
Relative to the baseline, the HEA will exhibit lower corrosion current density during tribo-corrosion.
Surface analysis will reveal a reformed, continuous passive film within worn regions.
The regenerative HEA may reduce total degradation by approximately 20–50%, primarily through a decrease in the corrosion-dominated mass-loss component.
The predicted benefit holds only when wear is moderate enough for oxide regeneration and electrolyte aggressiveness does not overwhelm repassivation.
At very high wear rates or in extremely aggressive electrolytes, passive-film self-healing may fail.
